verdict.reasoning: Headache duration and onset: patient says it started in the morning and ‘the headache started like four hours ago’; sudden onset: ‘Yeah, yeah, yeah’ to ‘Was it a sudden onset headache?’; left-sided: ‘It’s in one side. The left side only.’; intensity: ‘I have now maybe five. Well, six.’; dizziness: ‘I feel like dizzy.’
Visual changes: ‘My vision is quite blurred. It’s really weird. Like some zigzag lines kind of’; screen intolerance: ‘I cannot stand screens.’
Nausea/vomiting: ‘I forgot to mention, definitely I vomit twice, actually. As soon as the headache started… and I still feel nausea. I’m about to vomit very soon, I think.’
No prior similar headaches: ‘Have you ever had a headache like this in the past?’ / patient: ‘Well, not really because it’s a first. Yeah, like this? No, definitely it’s something new.’

No weakness or gait disturbance: doctor asks about weakness and walking; patient: ‘No, not it. No. No.’ and ‘Not really.’ Doctor summarizes: ‘you’ve got no neurological symptoms. You’re walking fine.’
Concern about serious causes: patient says they worry about ‘some kind of brain tumor or something… Or maybe a stroke… if I should go to A and E urgently… I might really have something serious.’
History of kidney stones: ‘Well, I had the kidney stone, so let’s say that that’s 10’; doctor later: ‘You’ve mentioned in the past you’ve had kidney stones.’
No regular meds: ‘Do you take any regular medications?’ / patient: ‘No.’
No known drug allergies: ‘Are you allergic to any medications?’ / patient: ‘Not that I’m aware. Yeah, not that I’m aware.’
Family history: ‘My mother has migraines…’ and ‘I have hypothyroidism in the family…’ clarified as ‘She also has hypothyroidism.’

The doctor explicitly says they have not yet done the ‘full neurological exam’: ‘we would want to see you as soon as possible to do like a full neurological exam as well.’ Only symptom-based absence is discussed; no objective examination findings are reported.
Intolerance of movement: ‘when I move like the thing is that if I leave bed I start to feel like even worse if I move. So I just want to have my head like really not moving.’

Migraine assessment: doctor states ‘it sounds like what you’re suffering from is what’s known as a migraine’; features described include ‘on one side of the head… blurry vision… nausea and vomiting,’ consistent with a unilateral headache with visual aura, nausea, and vomiting.
Ibuprofen plan: ‘I would recommend in the time between now and when we can see you take some medications, maybe something like ibuprofen.’

Antiemetic/anti-sickness: ‘So there’s lots of medication treatments. So they can be ibuprofen with an anti sickness which you can get from the pharmacy.’ This supports a plan to trial an antiemetic medication.
Sugary carbonated drink: ‘And also to drink a sugary carbonated drink, something like coke.’

The doctor plans ‘we would want to see you as soon as possible to do like a full neurological exam’ and ‘an assessment where we could see you today at some point,’ but there is no mention of a ‘neurology’ (specialist) assessment; it appears to be a GP or general assessment.

Safety netting: ‘Any further problems between now and your appointment, please do let us know.’ While not listing specific signs, it advises seeking further care if there are worsening problems, which reasonably covers symptom worsening or new concerning features.

Patient is told they can cancel ‘the appointment’ with the same service, not a specialist: ‘if you do take these medications and… you feel much better… you can cancel it. You can give us a call and cancel it.’ There is no mention of a ‘specialist’ appointment.
